cards.title: Anti-portfolio: products to avoid when selecting an FBA item
cards.summary: Reject cheap, seasonal, trendy, gated, and patented products before spending on inventory to avoid dead stock and price wars.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products for a new Amazon FBA listing before committing capital to inventory.
steps: Rule out cheap products (roughly under $10 retail): the source argues a $7–8 flimsy item generates bad reviews, invites low-barrier competitors, and lets PPC clicks of about $1 consume all profit within two or three clicks.
Reject seasonal and trend-driven items, which leave you holding unsellable inventory and paying long-term storage fees once demand passes.
Reject restricted/gated categories and patented products — the source reports having ordered inventory he then could not sell because Amazon blocked the category or the item was patented.
Treat these as elimination criteria first, before evaluating upside: the speaker claims applying them saves tens of thousands of dollars, and that getting product selection wrong means failure.
Note this is one seller's opinion and heuristic, not a platform rule; verify current category gating and IP status per item before ordering.
caveats: The $10 price floor and '$1/click' figure are illustrative from the source, not measured benchmarks.
Some sellers profitably run cheap or seasonal products; the source's guidance assumes a paid-PPC-led launch model.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Four viability criteria for a target FBA product
cards.summary: Target premium-priced products with 30%+ net margin, problem-solving function, and low brand dominance.
cards.use_when: Building the shortlist of products worth deeper keyword and competitor analysis for an Amazon launch.
steps: Require a net profit margin of 30% or more after landed cost (product, shipping, duties, taxes) and FBA fees; treat below 30% as a discard signal per the source.
Set a minimum retail price around $25+; the speaker says his most profitable items are over $30 because higher ticket absorbs PPC and margin pressure.
Confirm the product solves a specific problem — the source frames this as 'dollars follow value' — since a better-resolved problem drives reviews, credibility, and repeat demand.
Check brand dominance: avoid categories where one legacy brand owns most of the sales (the source's example is Adidas/Nike/Puma soccer balls) and prefer niches where sales are spread across sellers.
Write the margin math out per unit before sourcing; the source criticizes sellers who don't know their FBA fees or landed cost.
caveats: 30% net margin and $25 minimum price are the source's heuristics, not industry standards; they vary by category and business model.
Low brand dominance is judged qualitatively — the source gives no numeric threshold for 'spread out' sales.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Keyword variability test: count the ways a product is searched
cards.summary: Prefer products describable by many distinct long-tail keywords so you can rank on multiple first-page terms instead of one contested head term.
cards.use_when: Deciding between two candidate products, or judging whether a niche offers cheap organic entry for a new Amazon listing.
steps: Take your candidate product and list the distinct ways a customer might search for it — the source's phone-case example: slim, green, wallet, waterproof, for men, for women.
Prefer products with dozens or hundreds of descriptive variants; these give many low-hanging long-tail terms to target in listing copy and launch PPC.
Discard or downgrade products with only one or two monolithic keywords — ranking becomes a single contested battle with no cheap entry points.
For ecommerce merchandising, apply the same test when writing PDP titles and bullet copy: cover the distinct descriptive variants rather than repeating one head term.
Validate the actual search demand for each variant in a keyword tool before building the listing around it.
caveats: The source gives no numeric minimum for 'enough' keywords — 'dozens' and '10/20/30/100' are illustrative.
Keyword counts and search volumes change over time; re-verify before committing.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Price-disparity check on Page 1 search results
cards.summary: Discard products whose Page 1 prices are tightly clustered; prefer wide spreads so you do not compete solely on price.
cards.use_when: Validating a candidate product's pricing power before sourcing inventory for an Amazon listing.
steps: Search the product's main keyword on Amazon and record the price of the first-page organic listings.
Example of a bad result from the source: 'tongue scraper' showed Page 1 prices from $6.99 to $12.99 — a roughly $6 spread — meaning near-identical products compete only on price and reviews.
Example of a good result: the same kind of product appearing at $20 and $100 on Page 1, showing buyers pay for something other than lowest price.
Discard products where all Page 1 results sit in a narrow band (the source cites $7–$13 as a discard band).
Use the spread to inform your own pricing and differentiation strategy: wide spread means positioning, bundling, or quality upgrades can justify a higher price.
caveats: Prices on Page 1 shift with promotions, coupons, and seasonality; sample more than once.
Wide price spread does not guarantee you can occupy the high end — it signals room to try, not capacity to win.

cards.title: Helium 10 Black Box filter stack for finding weak competitors
cards.summary: A strict numeric filter set to isolate high-revenue, low-sophistication, ungated FBA competitors.
cards.use_when: Running a first-pass product scan in Helium 10 Black Box (Products tab) to generate raw candidates for an Amazon FBA launch.
steps: Open Helium 10 → Tools → Black Box → Products tab (verify the current interface, as tooling changes).

Set Category to an ungated one: the source names Home & Kitchen, Patio Lawn & Garden, Pet Supplies, Office Products, Industrial & Scientific, Kitchen & Dining, Sports & Outdoors, Tools & Home Improvement, and warns Baby, CDs/Vinyl, and some Electronics (batteries) cause gating problems.
Set Review Count Max = 300 to exclude dominant listings with tens of thousands of reviews.
Set Price = $25 to $60 (adjust upward with your budget) to avoid the cheap-product trap.
Set Monthly Revenue = $5,000 to $20,000 to cap the inventory and marketing capital required; the source warns a $30k/month product demands a large budget for stock and ads.
Set Listing Age Minimum = 8 months to filter out fads and validate evergreen demand.
Set Image Count Max = 4 to surface sellers with weak listings — the source calls sub-4-image sellers 'clueless' and therefore beatable.
The source's example run returned 500+ matching products; do not copy his exact filters wholesale — vary categories so you are not chasing the same products as everyone else.
caveats: These are the presenter's personal heuristics, not proven thresholds; the source explicitly says not to follow the exact filters.
Revenue and review estimates from any tool are modeled, not actual seller data.
Verify current filter names and availability in your Helium 10 subscription.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Review mining: turn 4.1–4.3 star sellers into a product spec
cards.summary: Sort results by lowest rating, find mediocre-but-selling products, and read 1-star reviews to extract the exact improvements to brief a supplier.
cards.use_when: Turning a shortlisted FBA candidate into a manufacturing brief before contacting suppliers.
steps: In Helium 10 Black Box results, sort by review rating from lowest to highest to surface products with real demand but unresolved quality problems.
Target products rated roughly 4.1–4.3 stars still generating over $5,000/month — they sell despite flaws, meaning fixes should lift conversion.

Open the 1-star reviews and read them for concrete physical complaints: fit, size, color options, durability, missing features. The source's example found a sun shade with 12% one-star reviews and photoshopped listing images.
Translate each recurring complaint into a specific requirement in your supplier brief (materials, dimensions, added options), then advertise the fix in your listing.
Repeat for your own post-launch PDP: mine 1–3 star reviews of competitors and of your own product to prioritize the next iteration.
caveats: The 4.1–4.3 / $5k thresholds are the source's heuristics, not tested benchmarks.
Some complaints reflect misuse or unrealistic buyer expectations rather than fixable defects — read for patterns, not single reviews.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Giftability and demand screening before committing to a product
cards.summary: Favor products that work as gifts for multiple holidays or for self-purchase, because Q4 and seasonal events add demand spikes.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing among otherwise-viable FBA candidates, especially when planning a launch calendar around Q4 or holidays.
steps: Ask whether the product works as a gift for Christmas, birthdays, Mother's/Father's Day, Easter, or Valentine's Day — the source calls this 'giftable' and says it is not mandatory but drives holiday sales spikes.
Prefer products that also sell as self-purchase so demand is not entirely seasonal-dependent — this reconciles with the source's separate rule against seasonal/trendy items.
Check the remaining baseline: high demand and low competition, which the source treats as the umbrella criterion the other tests feed into.
Align your sourcing and ad-spend calendar with the gift windows you identified so inventory lands before the spike.
Treat giftability as a tiebreaker between candidates, not a substitute for margin, keyword, and price-disparity checks.
caveats: Giftability alone does not overcome weak margins or a price race to the bottom.
Holiday demand peaks can also mean post-holiday inventory overhang — plan quantities accordingly.
cards.source_name: COMPLETE Amazon FBA Product Research Masterclass.docx

cards.title: Budget-matched revenue ceiling for new FBA sellers
cards.summary: Choose products whose monthly revenue matches the inventory and ad budget you can actually fund, not the biggest revenue number you can find.
cards.use_when: Setting the Monthly Revenue filter or choosing between candidates when planning first inventory buy-in for an FBA launch.
steps: Estimate capital required: matching, say, $30k/month in sales requires roughly three months of inventory plus substantial marketing spend, per the source.
New sellers with limited budgets should therefore filter to a lower revenue band — the source's example uses $5,000–$20,000/month — rather than chasing the highest-revenue product on the page.
Acknowledge the trade-off the source states outright: products doing only $1,500–$3,000/month can still be viable opportunities, just smaller.
Reverse-engineer the number: pick the revenue band whose inventory and ad cost your budget can sustain through at least one replenishment cycle.
Re-run Black Box filters with that band before falling in love with any single product.
caveats: The $1.5k–$20k bands are the source's illustrative examples, not formulas; compute your own landed cost and cash cycle.
Revenue estimates in third-party tools are approximations, not seller-verified figures.
